## Overview
<!--
At a high-level address what your proposal is and how it will address
the problem identified. Highlight any benefits to the R Community that
follow from solving the problem. This should be your most compelling
section.

Include concrete actions you will take and estimated timeline.
-->

The proposal is a Vale style for R package documentation, plus an R package, valer, that installs Vale, configures it and runs it, so documentation can be linted from R, from the command line or on CI.
It covers a package's vignettes and READMEs and the comments in its R source files, and reports the file, line, rule and a message explaining what was wrong.
For R that's a data frame, and for other tools, it's Vale's own JSON output.

Vale already has rules for sentence length and readability scores, spread across several styles and tuned for general prose.
This project would pick out the subset that makes sense for package documentation, set thresholds by running them over real packages so the defaults aren't noisy, and add a vocabulary of common R terms.
These become the default style, which ships with the package and is also published for people who use Vale directly.
Rules are configured from a Vale config file at the package root, which the package can generate, so people can turn things off or tighten them to taste.

Vale handles extracting comments from R files, parsing Markdown, running rules and integrating with editors, and because its rules are data rather than code, people can contribute rules without writing any R.
It also has an official GitHub Action and a pre-commit hook, so once the style is installable those work without any extra code, and the package documents how to use them.
This means there isn't much new code to write.

The package itself has three parts: finding an existing Vale binary or downloading one for the user's platform when asked, the way tinytex does; a setup function that writes the Vale config for a project and installs the style; and a function that runs Vale and returns lints as a data frame.
The setup function also writes a short block into the project's AGENTS.md telling AI coding agents to run the linter on any documentation they write and fix what it reports.
This means agents are checked against the same rules as everyone else.

The main dependency is Vale itself, which is actively maintained and publishes binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows on every release.
There are no ongoing costs.
